Adult Tawny frogmouths (Podargus strigoides) reach a total body length of approximately 43.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 43.5 centimeters], a dimension that places them among the larger members of the caprimulgiform order. Body mass data from wild-caught individuals in southeastern Australia indicate that the ultimate wet weight, or maximum adult body mass, averages 473.75 grams [Wwi = 473.75 grams], with males and females exhibiting only slight sexual dimorphism in this trait. This substantial size is reflected in their life history timing: incubation of the fertilised ovum proceeds over roughly 30 days [ab = roughly 30 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime reported in studies of captive breeding colonies (KuehGood1990; BechNico1999). The altricial nestlings that emerge weigh a mere 14 grams [Wwb = 14 grams] at birth, underscoring the energetic investment required during the subsequent brooding period.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, around 39.7 °C [T = around 39.7 °C], several key developmental milestones have been documented in longitudinal field studies. The downy chick reaches the fledging stage after approximately 32.5 days since birth [tx = approximately 32.5 days since birth], after which it remains dependent on parental provisioning for some time at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation in immature individuals, is attained at roughly 97.5 days since birth [tp = roughly 97.5 days since birth]; this relatively protracted juvenile phase may reflect the time required to develop the sophisticated camouflage and hunting skills essential for a nocturnal sit-and-wait predator at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C].

Reproductive output in Tawny frogmouths is modest but consistent with their large body size and extended parental care. Females typically lay a clutch of 2 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 2 eggs] per breeding event, and they produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a low annual fecundity that is offset by high adult survival. The first successful breeding event, or time since birth at first brood, occurs at approximately 240 days since birth [tR = approximately 240 days since birth] when birds are maintained at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This delayed onset of reproduction, combined with the modest clutch size, suggests a slow life-history pace typical of long-lived birds.

Longevity records from banding studies indicate that Tawny frogmouths can achieve a maximum lifespan of approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days] under field conditions, a figure that translates to roughly 40 years and is exceptional among caprimulgids of comparable size at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. At an active body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the species exhibits a resting metabolic rate that is consistent with the low energetic demands predicted for a bird that employs passive crypticity rather than active flight to evade predators. This combination of extreme longevity and low reproductive output positions the Tawny frogmouth as a textbook example of a slow life-history strategist within the Australasian avifauna.

Comparative analyses with closely related frogmouth species from New Guinea and the Solomon Islands reveal that Podargus strigoides exhibits the largest ultimate total length of the genus, achieving 43.5 cm [Li = 43.5 cm] in adults, a value that exceeds that of Podargus papuensis by several centimeters.
